title: A validated human intervention that greatly slows systemic aging

concept.text: The target innovation is a safe, practical human intervention that substantially delays multiple clinically important consequences of aging while preserving physical and cognitive function. It would act on aging biology broadly enough to produce a large, sustained benefit across several outcomes, rather than improving only one disease or changing an aging biomarker. The intervention could be a drug, a combination of treatments or another scalable modality. This is a proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its achievement in humans.

The biological motivation includes evidence that manipulating a signaling pathway can improve several aging-related traits and extend lifespan in mice. Inhibition of interleukin-11, or IL-11, provides one such example. That finding supports investigating shared mechanisms of aging, but translating a mouse intervention into broad, durable human benefit requires separate clinical evidence.

significance.text: Conditional significance: an intervention that substantially delays several age-related diseases and preserves function would expand medicine’s ability to address biological risks shared across late-life conditions. The IL-11 paper provides a rationale for this approach by linking chronic inflammation with senescence, frailty, metabolic dysfunction and multiple coexisting diseases. It does not establish that IL-11 inhibition delivers these benefits in humans.

Synthesis: the direct consequence of the stipulated clinical benefits would be a longer period of good health for treated people. Greater independence and reduced demand for some forms of late-life care would be plausible downstream possibilities, depending on the magnitude, duration, affordability and distribution of benefit. Neither longer healthspan nor delayed disease necessarily entails reversal of existing damage, prevention of every disease, a proportional increase in human lifespan or elimination of death.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability requires moving from modifiable aging-related traits in experimental animals to a large, sustained and acceptably safe effect across multiple human clinical outcomes. The supplied mouse study establishes a biological motivation for that work. It cannot establish whether a qualifying human intervention remains absent as of 1 November 2026, because no updated assessment of the field was supplied.

Engineering and clinical synthesis: the central barriers are selecting an intervention and treatment schedule whose effects translate to humans, showing that benefits extend across distinct diseases and functional outcomes, and determining whether those benefits outweigh harms over prolonged exposure. Practical success also requires a reproducible treatment that can be delivered at useful scale. Changes in inflammatory signaling, laboratory measurements or aging biomarkers would need to be connected to meaningful health outcomes rather than assumed to establish systemic slowing of aging.

Evidence-design synthesis: human validation must distinguish a broad effect on aging-related health from a benefit concentrated in one disease or one component of a combined endpoint. Long follow-up, clear endpoint definitions and adequate assessment of harms are needed to determine durability and net benefit. A trial protocol would also need numerical effect thresholds and a plan for handling multiple comparisons; these details are not supplied here.

current_state.text: Anissa A. Widjaja, Wei-Wen Lim and colleagues reported “Inhibition of IL-11 signalling extends mammalian healthspan and lifespan” in Nature on 17 July 2024, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07701-9. In mouse lifespan experiments, anti-IL-11 treatment beginning at 75 weeks of age and continuing until death increased median lifespan by 22.5% in males and 25% in females. These are reported mouse results, not estimates of human benefit.

Separate experiments administering anti-IL-11 to 75-week-old mice for 25 weeks reported improvements in metabolism and muscle function, along with reductions in aging biomarkers and frailty in both sexes. The paper also reported that genetic deletion of Il11 extended mouse lifespan by an average of 24.9% across sexes. Genetic deletion and antibody treatment are distinct interventions, and the fixed-duration health measurements should be distinguished from the treatment-until-death lifespan experiments. The paper described the magnitude of lifespan extension as not yet fully determined.

At publication in July 2024, the authors described anti-IL-11 therapy as being in early-stage clinical trials for fibrotic lung disease and proposed studying its effects on aging-related conditions in older people. That statement concerns a translational opportunity and trials for a particular disease; it does not demonstrate systemic slowing of human aging or establish long-term human safety.

Evidence scope: the supplied review verified the article’s identity and assessed its complete retained HTML text and methods, with no indicated truncation. Figure images, raw data and separately linked supplements were not independently inspected. The reported numerical findings are explicit in the reviewed text, but this record does not constitute an independent reanalysis or replication. No updated research assessment was supplied beyond this dated study, so the field’s status as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved. That limitation does not invalidate the July 2024 report.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: large randomized human trials would show a substantial, durable reduction in a prespecified range of distinct age-related clinical outcomes, together with preserved physical and cognitive function and an acceptable long-term risk profile. The source motivates assessing healthspan alongside lifespan, but these proposed human criteria are a reasoned extension of that goal, not an established standard stated by the paper.
completion_criteria.label: Substantial, durable clinical benefits with preserved function and acceptable risks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed trial requirements: investigators would specify the minimum clinically meaningful effects, endpoint definitions, follow-up duration and statistical treatment of multiple comparisons before evaluating results. Individual outcome results should make clear whether an apparent overall benefit is broad or driven mainly by one condition. Biomarker changes could support interpretation, but would not by themselves meet the proposed clinical demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified clinical trial criteria distinguish broad benefit from single-condition effects

completion_criteria.text: Proposed confirmation and practical boundaries: independent replication across populations, survival follow-up and continued monitoring for delayed harms would strengthen the evidence. Studies should define the ages, baseline health conditions, treatment schedules and delivery settings in which benefit is demonstrated, while assessing whether treatment can be provided reliably at scale. Finite trials could establish substantial breadth within tested populations and conditions; they could not prove universal benefit for every person, disease or circumstance.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication and monitoring define benefit boundaries and scalability

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — LON-01, “A predictive causal theory of mammalian aging”: a causal theory could guide intervention selection and predict effects across outcomes. LON-03 concerns demonstrated human efficacy and safety; a useful intervention could be validated before a comprehensive predictive theory exists, while a theory alone would not demonstrate clinical benefit.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-02, “Safe, repeatable rejuvenation of an aged human body”: rejuvenation concerns restoring an aged body toward a younger functional state. LON-03 concerns slowing the development of aging-related consequences. An intervention might contribute to both, but delayed deterioration would not by itself establish rejuvenation or safe repeatability.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-04, “A fast, validated surrogate for human longevity trials”: a reliable surrogate could accelerate evaluation of candidate interventions. LON-03 concerns the intervention’s actual clinical benefits. A rapidly changing biomarker would help only to the extent that its relationship to relevant human outcomes had been validated.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-05, “In-place repair of accumulated molecular damage in old tissues”: damage repair could be one route to broader benefits, but LON-03 does not require a particular repair mechanism. Clinical slowing of age-related decline would not alone establish that accumulated molecular damage had been repaired.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-06, “Transfer of exceptional longevity mechanisms between species”: mechanisms found in unusually long-lived species could supply candidate interventions. Transferring such a mechanism is a distinct achievement from demonstrating broad human benefit, and LON-03 could be achieved through an intervention that does not originate in another species.

Roster-based synthesis — LON-07, “Control of systemic aging signals through the circulation”: circulating signals could provide a route to effects across multiple tissues. LON-07 concerns control of those signals; LON-03 requires convincing human health outcomes. Signal changes alone would not demonstrate the clinical capability, which could also arise through other mechanisms.

unresolved_issues: Whether any intervention meets the proposed human capability as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no updated field assessment was supplied.
The human efficacy, appropriate treatment schedule and long-term safety of IL-11 inhibition for systemic aging are not established by the supplied evidence.
Numerical benefit thresholds, endpoint definitions, follow-up duration, multiplicity control and acceptable risk boundaries remain to be specified for a concrete trial proposal.
Independent replication and the figure, raw-data and supplementary evidence underlying the reported mouse findings were not assessed in the supplied review.

brief.title: A treatment that greatly slows aging throughout the body
possible: People could stay physically and mentally capable for longer while a practical, safe treatment substantially delays several diseases of aging. The benefit would last and reach across different health problems.
why: Medicine could address biological risks shared by several late-life diseases. Older people could gain greater independence and need less care.

sources.who: Anissa A. Widjaja, Wei-Wen Lim and colleagues
sources.showed: Blocking IL-11, a protein that promotes inflammation, extended mouse lifespan. Separate experiments improved muscle function and metabolism, the body's use of energy, and reduced frailty.
sources.quote: improves metabolism and muscle function, and reduces ageing biomarkers and frailty across sexes.
sources.cited_for: The mouse findings support investigating shared biological causes of aging.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish broad, lasting benefits or long-term safety in humans.

sources.who: Patrizia Pasanisi, Andreina Oliverio and colleagues
sources.showed: A randomized trial tested the diabetes drug metformin with or without a Mediterranean diet. Fewer major diseases occurred, but diabetes prevention fully explained the difference.
sources.quote: The differences were fully explained by the reduction of type 2 diabetes
sources.cited_for: An overall reduction in disease can come entirely from preventing a single condition.
sources.not_established: The trial did not demonstrate benefits across distinct diseases of aging.

sources.who: Christine G. Lee and the Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group
sources.showed: Among adults at high risk of diabetes, metformin and lifestyle changes prevented diabetes but did not reduce deaths overall or deaths from cancer or cardiovascular disease.
sources.quote: Although metformin and lifestyle modification prevented diabetes, neither strategy reduced all-cause, cancer, or cardiovascular mortality rates.
sources.cited_for: Preventing diabetes does not by itself demonstrate longer life.
sources.not_established: This follow-up did not establish a survival benefit from either approach in the population studied.

sources.who: William E. Kraus and the CALERIE Investigators
sources.showed: A randomized trial of eating fewer calories while maintaining adequate nutrition improved blood pressure, cholesterol and other disease risk factors in healthy, non-obese adults.
sources.quote: Two years of moderate caloric restriction significantly reduced multiple cardiometabolic risk factors in young, non-obese men and women.
sources.cited_for: Dietary changes can improve several measures associated with disease risk in humans.
sources.not_established: Improved risk factors do not establish lasting prevention of multiple diseases or preserved physical and mental function.

shown: Widjaja, Lim and colleagues showed that blocking an inflammatory protein could extend mouse lifespan and improve several aspects of health. These findings come from one research group.

Human trials have shown narrower benefits. Metformin prevented diabetes without demonstrating broader disease prevention or reduced deaths. The CALERIE investigators improved several disease risk factors by reducing calorie intake.
missing: Human trials need to demonstrate large, lasting benefits across distinct diseases while preserving physical and mental function.
Prolonged treatment needs to show that its benefits outweigh immediate and delayed harms.
Independent studies need to confirm who benefits and whether treatment can be delivered reliably at scale.

milestones.label: Lasting human benefits with preserved abilities and acceptable risks
milestones.explanation: Large human trials with randomly assigned treatment would have to show substantial, lasting reductions across distinct diseases, preserved physical and mental abilities, and acceptable risks. This would establish meaningful health benefits.

milestones.label: Trial criteria distinguish broad benefits from single-disease effects
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to define meaningful effects, outcomes, duration and statistical safeguards in advance, then report each outcome. This would reveal whether benefits span diseases or mostly reflect a single condition.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation establishes who benefits and practical delivery
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to confirm benefits across populations, track survival and delayed harms, and define effective schedules and delivery settings. This would establish the treatment's reach and practical limits.

uncertain: Whether blocking IL-11 can safely produce broad, lasting benefits in humans remains an open question.
The required size and duration of benefits, and the acceptable level of risk, still need concrete definitions.
Benefits within tested populations would not establish benefits for every person or every disease.

page.title: Geroscience-based extension of human healthspan
page.definition: An intervention targeting biological aging delays diseases across multiple age-related disease families and preserves physical and cognitive function in humans. Healthspan is the period of life spent free of disease and disability.

goal.need: WHO estimates for 2023 put global life expectancy at 73.3 years and healthy life expectancy at 62.8 years, a calculated gap of 10.5 years. Noncommunicable diseases accounted for 74% of deaths. These population measures quantify the health burden; they do not estimate how much an aging intervention could prevent.

figures.caption: Global life expectancy and healthy life expectancy in 2023
figures.note: Healthy life expectancy adjusts survival for time spent in less than full health. The difference is not an estimate of preventable aging.

completion.title: Replicated human trials demonstrate multidisease prevention with preserved physical and cognitive function.
completion.criterion: Independently replicated randomized controlled human evidence shows that the same intervention targeting aging biology delays incident disease across more than one age-related disease family and preserves physical and cognitive function, with a favorable clinical benefit–risk assessment. Effects must meet the trials' prespecified efficacy, multiplicity and safety criteria over their stated follow-up. A composite benefit entirely explained by one disease, or an aging-biomarker change alone, does not qualify. No universal minimum effect size, follow-up duration or numerical safety margin is established.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, informed by Geroscience Network goals, TAME outcome design and ARPA-H endpoint recommendations; not an adopted regulatory standard.
completion.basis: Searched FDA and EMA endpoint guidance, Geroscience Network/TAME designs, endpoint-consensus literature, ARPA-H's May 2026 framework and XPRIZE Healthspan rules. No common clinical threshold defining systemic human aging slowdown was found. TAME proposes disease and functional outcomes; XPRIZE tests functional restoration. This provisional clinical test follows the quoted multidisease goals without assigning a percentage change in aging rate.

milestones.title: A late-life intervention extends mouse survival at two-sided P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: In the published IL-11 lifespan experiment, compare survival of treated and control C57BL/6J mice using a two-sided log-rank test at P < 0.05. Treatment starts at 75 weeks; the endpoint includes natural death and protocol-defined humane euthanasia. The report published on 17 July 2024 tested monthly intraperitoneal anti-IL-11 at 40 mg/kg: 37 treated mice and 38 controls. Median lifespan increased by 22.5% in males and 25% in females. This establishes an animal result, not human geroprotection.
milestones.set_by: Widjaja and colleagues, published mouse lifespan protocol and statistical analysis; a study-specific preclinical benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: The criterion for statistical significance was set at P  <  0.05.

milestones.title: A candidate gerotherapeutic reaches human dosing with acute safety and dose tolerance characterized.
milestones.criterion: Meet the FDA's phase 1 objective of determining human dose tolerance and acute adverse effects; its typical participant ranges are descriptions, not passing thresholds. An early human example is the 2019 two-centre, uncontrolled study of dasatinib plus quercetin in 14 people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Participants received 100 mg/day dasatinib and 1,250 mg/day quercetin on three consecutive days weekly for three weeks. All completed dosing; one serious adverse event occurred. These observations do not establish long-term safety or systemic efficacy.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Step 3: Clinical Research, phase 1 objectives; general drug-development criteria.
milestones.threshold_quote: to find out how much of a drug the body can tolerate and what its acute side effects are.

milestones.title: A randomized human intervention improves cardiometabolic risk factors over two years.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate favorable changes in CALERIE's two-year exploratory cardiometabolic outcomes, including blood pressure, plasma lipids, inflammation and glucose regulation. CALERIE randomized 218 healthy adults aged 21–50 years to prescribed 25% calorie restriction or unrestricted intake: 143 versus 75 participants. The 2019 report found improvements in LDL cholesterol, cholesterol ratio and blood pressure, with reported P values below 0.002. These are risk-factor outcomes; the study did not establish reduced multidisease incidence.
milestones.set_by: CALERIE investigators, registered study NCT00427193 and published phase 2 analysis; a calorie-restriction benchmark, not a universal aging threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: Exploratory cardiometabolic risk factor responses to a prescribed 25% calorie restriction diet for 2 years were evaluated

milestones.title: An intervention reduces a composite of incident age-related diseases at two-sided P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: Reduce the MeMeMe composite incidence of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease or cancer versus control, using the published two-sided P < 0.05 rule. MeMeMe randomized 1,442 adults aged 50–79 years with metabolic syndrome; mean follow-up was 3 years. Metformin, 1,700 mg/day, reduced the composite, entirely through diabetes prevention; cardiovascular disease and cancer incidence were not reduced. Separately, DPP/DPPOS followed 3,234 randomized adults for a median 21 years: metformin did not reduce all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.79–1.25). Neither result establishes completion.
milestones.set_by: MeMeMe investigators, registered study NCT02960711 and published primary-outcome analysis; a study-specific clinical benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: A P value <0.05 was taken as significant. All statistical tests were two-sided.

not_found: No regulator-endorsed numerical definition combining the magnitude, duration and acceptable risks of systemic human aging slowdown was found.
No human result satisfying the completion criterion was found in the sources examined.
The NIA Geroscience Interest Group and Interventions Testing Program pages and AFAR's TAME page could not be retrieved.
The CALERIE and DPP/DPPOS full-text PMC pages were blocked; their PubMed abstracts were accessible.
